description: Hi! I’m a Computer Science Engineering student with a strong interest in Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Web Development, and innovative problem-solving. I enjoy building practical projects that combine technology with real-world applications, especially in areas like AI-powered systems, computer vision, data analysis, and intelligent automation. summary: MODIS has detected fires from space for 25 years but is scheduled to retire around 2026–27, and its successor VIIRS is not a drop-in replacement: its pixels are smaller, its overpass times differ, and its confidence values use a different scale. We built a pipeline that standardizes NASA FIRMS active-fire data from MODIS and two VIIRS satellites (NOAA-20, NOAA-21) into one format and merges them into a daily fire calendar on a ~2 km grid, labelling each cell MODIS-only, VIIRS-only or both, with a unified confidence score. Over central India (1–7 Nov 2026), VIIRS gave about 13 times more detections than MODIS (4,158 vs 314). 42% of MODIS fire cells had a VIIRS fire nearby the same day, against about 5% by chance, while only 8.5% of VIIRS cells were seen by MODIS. Even two VIIRS satellites agreed on only about a third of cells, so the combined calendar finds fires that any single sensor misses. An interactive dashboard lets users explore the results by day, sensor and day/night.
details:
What it does. The pipeline reads NASA FIRMS near-real-time active-fire data from MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (NOAA-20, NOAA-21, 375 m), converts them to one schema (UTC time, confidence on a 0–1 scale, FRP, pixel size), and merges the two VIIRS satellites. Detections are placed on a 0.02° (~2 km) grid for each UTC day, and each cell is labelled MODIS-only, VIIRS-only or both, with a unified confidence of 1 − (1 − c_MODIS)(1 − c_VIIRS). That formula is our own simple rule, not an official one. An interactive dashboard shows the calendar by day, sensor and day/night.

Findings (central India, 1–7 Nov 2026; agreement statistics use full days, 2–6 Nov). VIIRS gave 4,158 detections vs 314 for MODIS. 42% of MODIS fire cells (47% by day) had a VIIRS fire within about 2 km the same day, against about 4–5% in a control with VIIRS shifted by 0.5°. Only 8.5% of VIIRS cells were seen by MODIS. As a reference level, the two VIIRS satellites agreed on only 30–37% of each other’s cells, probably because of different pass times and short-lived fires (we did not test this). MODIS saw more VIIRS fires as fire intensity rose, from 3.8% under 2 MW to about 23% at 32–64 MW (the top bin has only 22 cells).

Why it matters. MODIS is scheduled to retire, and fire records need to stay consistent across the switch. The calendar shows where the sensors agree, where only VIIRS sees a fire (2,820 cells) and where only MODIS does (249 cells), so one sensor’s gaps are not mistaken for fire-free areas.

Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy), Leaflet, Esri basemap tiles, NASA FIRMS data.

Limitations. One week and one region. Agreement between sensors is not validated against reference fire records. Matching uses the UTC date, not exact overpass time. MODIS has only 52 night detections in our data, so night results are indicative. The grid size and confidence rule are design choices.

Team and SI use. The Cosmic Coders (Hyderabad) chose the problem, collected the NASA FIRMS data, and ran, tested and interpreted all analyses. An SI (AI) assistant was used to help write the code and draft text, and the team reviewed and edited the results.
